subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Supernovae: Exploding Stars
description: A quick, practical guide to Supernovae: Exploding Stars.

hook.text: When a massive star dies, it explodes with the energy of an entire galaxy—briefly outshining billions of stars.

buildup.text: The core runs out of fuel and collapses in milliseconds. The outer layers slam inward, then rebound outward.

discovery.text: In 1054, Chinese astronomers recorded a guest star so bright it was visible in daylight for 23 days.

twist.text: Supernovae forge elements heavier than iron—gold, platinum, uranium. Every heavy atom on Earth was born this way.

climax.text: The remnant of the 1054 supernova is the Crab Nebula. At its center spins a neutron star 30 times per second.

punchline.text: Stars die to make gold. We are built from their debris.

quiz.question: Where do elements heavier than iron, like gold and uranium, come from?
options: They are forged in the extreme energy of supernova explosions
They form slowly inside the cores of red giant stars
They are created by cosmic rays bombarding interstellar dust

details.summary: Supernovae are cataclysmic explosions marking the deaths of massive stars or the detonation of white dwarfs. For weeks, a single supernova can outshine an entire galaxy. These explosions forge elements heavier than iron and blast them into space, seeding future generations of stars and planets.
details.whyItMatters: Every atom of gold, silver, and uranium in your body was created in a supernova. These explosions are the universe's heavy-element factories and the engines of cosmic chemical evolution.
takeaways: Supernovae can briefly outshine an entire galaxy
They forge elements heavier than iron and disperse them
They're the deaths of massive stars or detonating white dwarfs

faq.question: What triggers a core-collapse supernova?
faq.answer: When a massive star's core fuses iron, fusion can no longer release energy. The core abruptly collapses in milliseconds, rebounds off the ultra-dense core, and blasts the outer layers into space. The collapse releases more energy in seconds than the Sun will produce in its entire lifetime.

faq.question: How often do supernovae occur in our galaxy?
faq.answer: About one to two per century in the Milky Way, though many are hidden behind dust. The last supernova visible to the naked eye from Earth was Kepler's Supernova in 1604. Betelgeuse and Eta Carinae are considered candidates for the next nearby supernova.
